How do you do? Introductions, frequency, purpose

Hello! My name is Maria Lopez. I'm from Mexico. I'm studying Korean to get a job at a Korean company, but speaking is still hard for me. I'm looking for someone to meet about twice a week and talk in Korean. I can teach you Spanish. I'm free on weekday evenings or at weekends. Contact: maria@mail.com

Korean names usually have three syllables. The first is the family name; Kim, Lee and Park are the most common. When calling someone by name, Koreans drop the family name and use the given name only, or add “씨”. At work people use the family name plus the job title instead, like “Manager Kim”.
The most polite “Nice to meet you (for the first time)”. **뵙다** is the humble form of 보다/만나다 (used when meeting someone respected).
After a consonant **이라고 하다**, after a vowel **라고 하다**. Used for names and for what things are called.
What is this called in Korean?
A form asks for: **성명** (full name), **성별** (sex), **생년월일** (date of birth), **국적** (nationality), **주소** (address), **연락처** (contact), **종교** (religion).

How do I call you (by what name)?

**항상** always > **자주** often > **가끔** sometimes > **별로 안** rarely > **전혀 안** never. **매일/매주/매달/매년** = every day/week/month/year.
Stem + **-거나** joins two alternative actions or states: **보거나**, **읽거나**. The tense is at the end.

When I have time, I meet friends or just rest at home.

Vowel stem (and ㄹ) + **-려고**, consonant stem + **-으려고**, then any verb: 한국 회사에 **들어가려고** 공부해요.
I walk every day to lose weight.
**-(으)러** only before movement verbs (가다, 오다…); **-(으)려고** before any verb. Neither can be followed by -(으)세요 / -(으)ㄹ까요.
N에 대해서 = about N: 한국 문화에 대해서 발표했어요.

After a vowel **나**, after a consonant **이나**: 커피**나** 차, 빵**이나** 과일. (For verbs it was -거나.)

**N 정도** = about N: 두 시간 **정도** (about two hours), 열 명 **정도** (about ten people).
제일 = the most: 제일 친한 친구 (my closest friend).

What's your hobby? Hobbies, skills, clubs

My hobby is taking photos. Last year I joined a photography club. The members meet twice a month and go out to take pictures together. Last week I posted the photos I took on my blog. At first I didn't know how to take good photos, but now it's not that hard. Join us too!
Latin dance club — new members wanted! It's fine if you can't dance. When: every Saturday 3 pm. Where: culture centre, 2nd floor practice room. Fee: 20,000 won a month.
Turning a verb into a noun: V-는 것
Verb stem + **-는 것** = “doing …” (the activity as a noun). In speech **것** → **거**, and with particles: 것이 → **게**, 것을 → **걸**, 것은 → **건**.
Many hobbies are nouns already: **독서** (reading), **등산** (hiking), **낚시** (fishing), **영화 감상** (watching movies), **음악 감상** (listening to music).
ㄹ-stems: 만들다 → 만드는 것, 살다 → 사는 것.
My hobby is playing computer games.
What is your hobby? Use V-는 것.
Know how to: V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다/모르다
Vowel stem (and ㄹ) + **-ㄹ 줄 알다**, consonant stem + **-을 줄 알다**. It means knowing **how** to do something (a skill). Negative: **-(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다**.
I can speak three foreign languages.
I don't know how to dance Latin dances.
**-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다** = a learned skill only. **-(으)ㄹ 수 있다** = skill **or** possibility: 오늘 갈 수 있어요 (I can go today), but not ~~갈 줄 알아요~~.
-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 is about skills, not about having time.
How many foreign languages can you speak?
Do you need to know how to dance to join?

Something done in the past: V-(으)ㄴ N
Verb stem + **-ㄴ** (vowel) / **-은** (consonant) + noun = the noun that was done: **어제 본 영화** (the movie I watched yesterday), **찍은 사진** (the photo I took).
The movie I saw yesterday was fun.
It's the club I joined last year.
For **adjectives** -(으)ㄴ means **present**: 큰 집 (a big house). For **verbs** it means **past**: 간 곳 (a place I went).
모이다 = to gather; 회비 = membership fee; 연습실 = practice room.
The song I heard yesterday was good.
The place where we gathered is the culture centre.

Stem + **-지 않아요** = 안 + verb: 가지 않아요 = 안 가요. It's a bit more formal and common in writing. Past **-지 않았어요**.
**아주 / 참** very; **별로 + negative** not really; **전혀 + negative** not at all.
How's studying Korean? — Not that hard.
별로 and 전혀 always need a negative: ~~별로 좋아요~~ → 별로 안 좋아요.

Vowel stem (and ㄹ) + **-니까**, consonant stem + **-으니까**, noun + **(이)니까**. Past: **-았/었으니까**.

Before **-(으)세요, -(으)ㄹ까요, -(으)ㅂ시다** use only **-(으)니까**: ~~비가 와서 우산을 가지고 가세요~~ → 비가 **오니까** 우산을 가지고 가세요. -아서/어서 can't take the past; -(으)니까 can.

Verb stem + **-고 나서** = after (completely) doing …: 밥을 먹**고 나서** 산책해요. It stresses that the first action is finished.
After finishing grad school I want to travel.
After saving money I'll buy a car.
After doing homework I play games.
**-고** — just “and then”; **-고 나서** — clearly “after finishing”; **-아서/어서** — the actions are connected (same place/object).
바라다 = to hope, wish (formal): 건강하시길 바랍니다.
After grad school I want to work in Korea.
After saving money I'll travel the world.
After eating, let's take a walk.
After quitting smoking I feel healthier.

Before a **request, command or suggestion** use **-(으)니까**: 시간이 없**으니까** 택시를 탑시다. -(으)니까 may also take the past: 많이 걸**었으니까** 좀 쉬세요. -아서/어서 cannot do either, but it is what you use with 고맙다, 미안하다, 반갑다: 도와줘**서** 고마워요.

1. ~~비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요~~ → 비가 **오니까** 우산을 가져가세요. 2. ~~덥으니까~~ → 더**우니까**; ~~살으니까~~ → **사니까**; ~~듣으니까~~ → 들**으니까**. 3. -고 나서 goes with verbs only, and the first action must be finished: 밥을 먹**고 나서** 이를 닦아요. 4. A guess about another person or thing is -(으)ㄹ 거예요; a promise about yourself is -(으)ㄹ게요.

Write a recommendation of a place to travel to: why it suits your friend (-(으)니까), what it will probably be like (-(으)ㄹ 거예요), where to stay and how much it costs, and the order of two things to do there (-고 나서).

Before -아/어, **르** loses ㅡ and a second **ㄹ** is added: 모르다 → 몰**라**요, 부르다 → 불**러**요. Before a consonant nothing changes: 모르**고**, 모**릅**니다, 모르**면**.

1. ~~모르어요~~ → 몰**라**요; ~~빠라요~~ → 빨**라**요. 2. ~~학생라서~~ → 학생**이라서**; ~~친구이라서~~ → 친구**라서**. 3. -(으)면 되다 says what is enough; -아/어야 되다 says what is required: 여기에 이름만 쓰**면 돼요**. 4. ~~도착하는 것 같아요~~ (already) → 도착**한** 것 같아요. 5. ~~우편로~~ → 우편**으로**; 배**로**, 택배**로**.

나가다 = go out (away from the speaker), 나오다 = come out (towards the speaker).

Verb stem + **-다가** = while doing A, (stop and) do B: 쭉 가**다가** 왼쪽으로 돌아가세요 (go straight, then turn left). The subject is the same; A gets interrupted.

Go straight along this road, pass the bank and go right.
**-고**: A is finished, then B. **-다가**: B starts in the middle of A. 밥을 먹**고** 전화했어요 (after eating) vs 밥을 먹**다가** 전화했어요 (in the middle of eating).

Most feelings are adjectives: **기쁘다, 슬프다, 외롭다, 즐겁다, 창피하다**. Some are verb phrases: **화가 나다** (get angry), **짜증이 나다** (get irritated), **걱정되다** (be worried), **긴장되다** (be nervous).
I'm nervous because of the exam.
My friend came late, so I got irritated.
ㅂ-irregular: 외롭다 → **외로워요**, 즐겁다 → **즐거워요**. ㅡ-drop: 기쁘다 → **기뻐요**, 슬프다 → **슬퍼요**, 나쁘다 → **나빠요**.

Because of: N 때문에 · A/V-기 때문에
Noun + **때문에** = because of N: 비 **때문에**, 시험 **때문에**. Verb/adjective + **-기 때문에** = because …: 늦게 일어났**기 때문에**. It sounds firm, a bit formal; not used before commands or suggestions.
I got up late, so I missed the bus.
I dozed off and went all the way to the last stop.
The roads are jammed because of the snow.
**시험 때문에** — because of the exam (the exam causes it); **학생이라서** — because I am a student (identity).
때문이에요 at the end: 늦은 건 비 때문이에요 (It's because of the rain).

Verb stem + **-아/어 버리다** = the action is completely done — often with regret (it's gone!) or relief (finally got rid of it): 버스가 **가 버렸어요** (the bus has gone!), 숙제를 다 **해 버렸어요** (I got the homework out of the way).
I've completely forgotten the words I memorised.
I lost my wallet, so I'm upset.
I was hungry, so I ate the whole cake by myself.
잃어버리다 (to lose) and 잊어버리다 (to forget) are written as one word.
I lost my wallet on the subway.
I was so tired that I fell asleep in class.
What happened on the way home?
the younger sibling ate all my cake — angry

Stem + **-(으)ㄹ 때** = when …: 힘들 **때**, 시간이 있**을 때**, 어렸**을 때** (when I was young). Noun + **때**: 방학 **때**, 점심 **때**.
When I first came to Korea, I was often at a loss.
When I'm lonely, I call a friend.
**때** — a point in time (when); **동안** — a duration (during, for): 방학 **때** 여행했어요 / 방학 **동안** 여행했어요 (the whole holiday).
“When I was a child” = 어렸을 때 (past form!).

you must be …; it must be …
Adjectives: 기쁘다, 슬프다, 외롭다, 속상하다, 답답하다, 창피하다. With **되다**: 걱정되다, 긴장되다. With **나다**: 짜증이 나다, 화가 나다. And 스트레스를 **받다** / **풀다**.

1. -겠- here is a guess about the **other** person's feeling: 힘들**겠어요**; about yourself say 힘들어요. 2. N 때문에 = because of N; N(이)라서 = because it **is** N: 비 **때문에** 못 갔어요 · 휴일**이라서** 쉬어요. 3. After -기 때문에 there is no command or suggestion — use -(으)니까. 4. ~~잊어 버렸어요~~ is written 잊어**버렸어요**; 가 버리다, 먹어 버리다 keep the same idea of “gone”. 5. Past moment: 어렸**을 때**.

In the middle of: V-는 중이다 · N 중이다
Verb stem + **-는 중이다** = be in the middle of …: 지금 통화하**는 중이에요**. Noun + **중이다**: 회의 **중**, 수업 **중**, 공사 **중**, 운전 **중**.
I'm in a meeting now, so I can't answer the phone.
Both mean “now doing”, but **-는 중이다** stresses being busy / in a process; it's not used with natural states (~~비가 오는 중이에요~~ is odd → 비가 오고 있어요).
Signs: 공사 중 (under construction), 회의 중 (meeting in progress), 영업 중 (open).

Verb/있다/없다 + **-나요?**, adjective + **-(으)ㄴ가요?**, noun + **인가요?**, past + **-았/었나요?** They sound softer and more careful than -아/어요?, good for enquiries.
**대상** — who it's for; **장소** — venue; **참가비** — entry fee; **재료비** — material fee; **접수** — registration; **문의** — enquiries; **무료** — free; **선착순** — first come, first served.

Noun + **밖에** + negative (안/못/없다/모르다) = only, nothing but — with the feeling “not enough”: 시간이 십 분**밖에 없어요** (I only have ten minutes).
There are only two places left.
I can only speak a little Korean.
**만** is neutral and goes with positive verbs: 물만 마셔요. **밖에** always takes a negative: 물밖에 안 마셔요. Never: ~~물밖에 마셔요~~.
